title: What Is ARFID? The Eating Disorder That More Than Tripled in Four Years – and Why So Few People Recognize It
summary: ARFID diagnoses more than tripled in the last 5 years. A therapist explains what avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder is, how it differs from picky eating, and how it’s treated.
body_markdown:
## When to Seek Help for ARFID


A helpful question is not, “Is this bad enough?” but “Is food getting in the way of health or daily life?” Ordinary picky eating tends to stay in the background, ARFID does not. Left unaddressed, it can lead to real medical consequences, and some warning signs that call for prompt professional or medical attention rather than a wait-and-see approach.


The following signs go beyond typical picky eating and warrant evaluation by a medical or mental health professional:


- Noticeable weight loss, or in children and teens, failure to gain weight or grow as expected (faltering growth)
- A range of accepted foods that keeps shrinking over time rather than expanding
- Signs of nutritional deficiency such as persistent fatigue, dizziness, hair thinning, brittle nails, or frequent illness
- Reliance on nutritional or oral supplement drinks to meet basic daily needs
- Feeling cold much of the time, poor concentration, or slow wound healing, which can signal malnutrition
- Gastrointestinal problems linked to limited intake, such as ongoing constipation or stomach pain
- In adolescents, delayed puberty or missed menstrual periods
- Fainting, lightheadedness, or a racing or irregular heartbeat, which can reflect the effects of undernutrition on the heart
- Intense fear of choking, vomiting, or getting sick that leads to skipping meals or near-total food refusal
- Meals routinely marked by dread, anxiety, or avoidance that disrupts school, work, relationships, or the ability to travel


Fainting, chest symptoms, a very low or irregular heartbeat, or rapid weight loss are urgent and should prompt same-day medical care rather than a routine appointment. For persistent food avoidance that is narrowing a person’s diet, health, or daily life, an evaluation is the right next step. Support tends to be most effective when it begins earlier rather than later.


[ARFID and other eating disorders](https://www.nimh.nih.gov/health/topics/eating-disorders) are treatable conditions, and reaching out is a sign of strength rather than weakness. Anyone who wants support or is unsure where to begin can contact the National Alliance for Eating Disorders helpline at 1-866-662-1235 to speak with a licensed clinician about next steps. If you’re looking for ongoing care, you can also reach out to a[LifeStance provider](https://lifestance.com/provider/) .
